column9: stem
column14: option_a
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: What is a mutation?
column14: Any change in the sequence of bases in DNA
column15: A protein that a ribosome builds
column16: An exact copy of DNA made before a cell divides
column17: A trait that is always harmful
column28: A mutation is any change in the DNA base sequence. Saying it is always harmful is the common mistake: many mutations are neutral and a few are helpful.
column29: Think about what the word mutate means in everyday language.

column9: Which kind of mutation replaces one base in DNA with a different base?
column14: Insertion
column28: A substitution swaps one base for another, so the gene stays the same length. An insertion adds a base, a deletion removes one, and a translocation moves a piece of a chromosome.
column29: In sports, a substitute takes another player's place. Which mutation does the same with a base?

column9: A mutation that adds one extra base into a DNA sequence is called a(n) ___.
column28: Adding a base is an insertion. Writing deletion is the common mix-up: a deletion removes a base.
column29: You insert a key into a lock. Is something being added or taken away?

column9: While a skin cell copies its DNA, one base is skipped, so the new copy of the gene is one base shorter. What kind of mutation is this?
column14: Insertion
column28: Losing a base is a deletion. A substitution keeps the same number of bases, and a duplication copies a piece, so neither one makes the gene shorter.
column29: The gene got shorter. Which mutation takes something away?

column9: Which term is another name for a mutation that changes just one base?
column14: Point mutation
column28: A change at a single point (one base) is a point mutation. Chromosomal mutations, such as translocations and duplications, change big pieces of a chromosome.
column29: The change happens at one tiny spot in the DNA.

column9: A single-base substitution happens inside a gene. Which effects on the protein could it have? Select all that apply.
column14: No change to the protein
column17: Every amino acid after the mutation changes
column18: A piece of the chromosome flips backward
column28: A substitution changes only one codon, so it can be silent (no change), missense (one amino acid changes) or nonsense (early stop). It can't shift the reading frame, which is the common mistake, and flipping a chromosome piece is an inversion.
column29: A substitution changes only one codon. List what can happen to that one codon.

column9: A point mutation that turns a codon for an amino acid into a stop codon is called a ___ mutation.
column28: It is a nonsense mutation: the early stop codon cuts the protein short. Missense is the common mix-up, but missense swaps one amino acid for another and the protein keeps going.
column29: Think about what a stop codon does to the message, and which mutation name says the message stops making sense.

column9: A substitution changes a codon, but the new codon still codes for the same amino acid. What is this called?
column14: Missense mutation
column28: When the amino acid stays the same, the protein doesn't change, so the mutation is silent. Missense is the common mistake, but missense means a different amino acid.
column29: If the protein is exactly the same, would anyone notice this mutation?

column9: In which type of cell would a mutation be passed on to a person's children?
column14: A skin cell
column28: Only mutations in sex cells (eggs and sperm) end up in offspring. Mutations in body cells like skin, muscle or liver stay in that person; thinking every mutation is inherited is the common mistake.
column29: Which cells actually join together to start a baby?

column9: Why are some substitutions silent?
column14: Many amino acids are coded for by more than one codon
column15: Ribosomes skip over any codon that has a mutation
column16: The cell always repairs the mRNA before translation
column17: Stop codons undo the mutation at the end of the gene
column28: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have several codons. A change from one of these codons to another gives the same amino acid. Ribosomes don't skip mutated codons; they read whatever is there.
column29: Compare the number of codons (64) to the number of amino acids (20).

column9: Which of these mutations causes a frameshift?
column14: Substituting one base for another
column17: A substitution that makes a stop codon
column28: Adding (or removing) one base shifts how all the following bases are grouped into codons. Every kind of substitution keeps the codons lined up, which is the common mistake: even a nonsense substitution changes only one codon.
column29: Codons are read in groups of three. Which change throws off the grouping?

column9: A deletion removes exactly three bases, one whole codon, from the middle of a gene. How many amino acids are missing from the protein? (Enter a number.)
column28: Three bases make one codon, and one codon codes for one amino acid, so one amino acid is lost and the rest of the protein reads normally. Thinking this causes a frameshift is the common mistake: removing a full codon keeps the reading frame.
column29: How many bases are in one codon, and how many amino acids does one codon code for?

column9: Something in the environment that can cause mutations, such as X-rays or certain chemicals, is called a(n) ___.
column28: A mutagen is anything that causes mutations. Carcinogen is a close miss: carcinogens cause cancer, often because they are mutagens, but the general word for a mutation-causer is mutagen.
column29: Its name starts the same way as the word mutation.

column9: Which of these are mutagens that can damage DNA? Select all that apply.
column14: Ultraviolet (UV) light
column28: UV light, X-rays and chemicals in tobacco smoke can all damage DNA. Loud sound can damage your hearing, but it doesn't change DNA, which is the common trap.
column29: Look for things that carry a lot of energy or are known to cause cancer.

column9: Even with no mutagens around, mutations still happen. What is one natural cause?
column14: Mistakes made while DNA is being copied
column28: When DNA is copied before a cell divides, the copying enzyme sometimes puts in the wrong base. Most of these errors are fixed, but a few become mutations. Diet, exercise and sleep don't directly rewrite DNA bases.
column29: Think about what happens to DNA every time a cell gets ready to divide.

column9: A lifeguard spends all summer outdoors. Which choice would best protect the DNA in their skin cells from mutations?
column14: Wearing sunscreen and a hat
column28: Sunscreen and clothing block UV light, the mutagen in sunlight that damages skin cell DNA. Water and diet don't block UV, which is the common mix-up between staying healthy and blocking a mutagen.
column29: What in sunlight damages DNA, and what blocks it?

column9: Which statement about the effects of mutations is correct?
column14: Mutations can be harmful, neutral or helpful
column17: Mutations only happen in people who are sick
column28: Mutations can hurt, have no effect, or even help an organism. Saying all mutations are harmful is the most common mistake; many are neutral, and helpful ones add the variation evolution works on.
column29: Could a mutation that doesn't change the protein at all be harmful?

column9: Every mutation in a gene changes the protein that the gene codes for.
column28: False. A silent mutation changes a codon into another codon for the same amino acid, so the protein stays the same. Assuming every DNA change shows up in the protein is the common mistake.
column29: Remember that some amino acids have more than one codon.

column9: A piece of a chromosome breaks off and is lost. Which chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Deletion
column28: Losing a piece is a deletion. A duplication copies a piece, an inversion flips one, and a translocation moves one to another chromosome.
column29: The piece is gone for good.

column9: A section of a chromosome breaks out, flips around, and reattaches in reverse order. Which chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Duplication
column28: Flipping a section backward is an inversion: the same genes are there, just in reverse order. Translocation is the common mix-up, but that moves a piece to a different chromosome.
column29: To invert something is to turn it upside down.

column9: A piece of one chromosome breaks off and attaches to a different, non-matching chromosome. Which chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Inversion
column28: Moving a piece to a different chromosome is a translocation. An inversion stays on the same chromosome and just flips the piece.
column29: Trans- means across, like transferring to a different school.

column9: Each letter stands for a gene. A normal chromosome reads ABCDEFGH. After a mutation it reads ABEFGH. What happened?
column14: Deletion
column28: Genes C and D are missing, so a piece was deleted. An inversion would still have all eight genes, just in a different order.
column29: Count the letters before and after.

column9: A normal chromosome reads ABCDEFGH (each letter is a gene). A mutated copy reads ABCDCDEFGH. Which chromosomal mutation is this?
column14: Deletion
column28: The section CD appears twice in a row, so it was duplicated. Calling it new genes from somewhere else is the common mistake; these are extra copies of genes already on the chromosome.
column29: Look for any letters that show up more than once.

column9: Which molecule carries a mutation's change from the DNA in the nucleus out to the ribosome?
column14: mRNA
column28: The gene is transcribed into mRNA, so the mRNA carries the changed codon to the ribosome. tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome but isn't a copy of the gene, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Which molecule is the messenger copy of a gene?

column9: Original DNA: ATG CCA TTG. Mutated DNA: ATG CGA TTG. Which type of mutation happened?
column14: Substitution
column28: Both sequences have nine bases, and only the C in the middle of the second triplet became a G. One base swapped for another is a substitution. If the length had changed, it would be an insertion or deletion.
column29: Count the bases in each sequence, then compare them one at a time.

column9: Original DNA: GAT TAC CAG. Mutated DNA: GAT TAC CCA G. Which type of mutation happened?
column14: Substitution
column28: The mutated DNA has 10 bases instead of 9 because an extra C was added: an insertion. It looks like several bases changed because the triplets after the extra C are regrouped, which is why people mistake it for substitutions.
column29: Count the bases. Did the sequence get longer, shorter or stay the same?

column9: A gene in a tomato plant normally reads TTA GCA CGT. A mutated copy reads TTA GAC GT. Which type of mutation happened?
column14: Insertion
column28: The mutated copy has 8 bases instead of 9 because the C in the second triplet is gone: a deletion. The leftover bases regroup into new triplets, so it can look like substitutions, which is the common mistake.
column29: Count the bases in each version.

column9: Put these events in order to show how a mutation can change a trait.
column14: The protein folds into a different shape and works differently
column15: The base sequence of a gene changes
column16: The trait of the organism changes
column17: The mRNA copied from the gene carries the change
column18: The ribosome builds a chain with a different amino acid sequence
column28: DNA → mRNA → protein → trait. The change starts in the gene, is copied into mRNA, is translated into a different amino acid chain, and the changed protein changes the trait. Putting the protein before the mRNA is the common mistake.
column29: Follow the path of information: DNA to RNA to protein.

column9: A student models a gene with a sentence of three-letter words: THE RED FOX ATE THE HEN. After a mutation it reads THE RED BOX ATE THE HEN. Which mutation does this model?
column14: Substitution
column28: One letter (F) was swapped for another (B), and every other word still reads the same, just like a substitution changes one base and only one codon. A frameshift would scramble every word after the change.
column29: Is the sentence the same length? How many words changed?

column9: In a bean plant gene, the mRNA codon GGU changes to GGA. A codon chart shows that both GGU and GGA code for glycine (Gly). What happens to the protein?
column14: Nothing changes, because the amino acid is still Gly
column15: Gly is replaced by a different amino acid
column16: The protein stops at this codon
column17: Every amino acid after this codon changes
column28: Both codons code for Gly, so the protein is identical: a silent mutation. Assuming any base change must change the amino acid is the common mistake.
column29: Check what each codon codes for before deciding.

column9: A substitution changes the mRNA codon AAA (lysine, Lys) to AGA (arginine, Arg). What type of mutation is this?
column14: Silent
column28: One amino acid is swapped for another (Lys to Arg) and the protein keeps its length: missense. It isn't silent because the amino acid changed, and it isn't nonsense because AGA is not a stop codon.
column29: Did the amino acid change? Is the new codon a stop?

column9: In a gene, the mRNA codon CAG (glutamine, Gln) changes to UAG. UAG is a stop codon. What happens to the protein?
column14: It is identical to the normal protein
column15: Gln is replaced by a different amino acid
column16: It ends at that spot, so it is shorter than normal
column28: A stop codon tells the ribosome to quit, so the protein ends early: a nonsense mutation. Thinking the stop codon just swaps in a new amino acid (missense) is the common mistake; stop codons don't code for any amino acid.
column29: What does a stop codon tell the ribosome to do?

column9: What usually happens to the amino acids that come after a one-base insertion in a gene?
column14: Almost all of them change, because the codons are regrouped
column15: Only the one amino acid at the insertion changes
column17: One extra amino acid is added and the rest stay the same
column28: One extra base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is grouped differently and most amino acids change (often an early stop shows up). Thinking an insertion just adds one amino acid is the common mistake; that only happens when three bases are added.
column29: Codons are read three bases at a time with no spaces. What happens to every group after one extra letter?

column9: Which example describes a mutation that helps the organism that has it?
column14: A mutation lets a bacterium survive an antibiotic that kills other bacteria
column15: A mutation makes a lung protein stop early so it can't work
column16: A mutation in a skin cell makes it divide out of control
column17: A frameshift breaks an enzyme a plant needs to make chlorophyll
column28: Surviving an antibiotic is a big advantage for the bacterium, so that mutation is helpful to it (even though it's bad news for people treating infections). The others break a protein or cause uncontrolled division, which harms the organism.
column29: Ask which mutation would help the organism survive and reproduce.

column9: Sickle cell disease is caused by a single base substitution in the hemoglobin gene. The protein is still full length, but one amino acid is different. What type of mutation is this?
column14: Silent
column28: One amino acid is replaced and the protein is full length, which is a missense mutation. That single change makes hemoglobin clump and red blood cells bend into a sickle shape, a reminder that one base can matter a lot.
column29: One amino acid swapped, nothing cut short.

column9: A student uses the sentence THE BIG DOG SAW THE CAT as a model of a gene. If the first E is deleted and the letters are regrouped in threes, how does the sentence read?
column14: THB IGD OGS AWT HEC AT
column15: THE BIG DOG SAW THE CAT
column16: TH BIG DOG SAW THE CAT
column17: THE BIG HOG SAW THE CAT
column28: Removing one letter shifts every group of three after it: THB IGD OGS AWT HEC AT. This is how a frameshift works in DNA. Keeping the other words whole (TH BIG DOG...) is the common mistake; cells read codons in threes with no spaces.
column29: Write the letters with no spaces, cross out the first E, then split into groups of three.

column9: A single chromosomal mutation, such as a large deletion, can affect many genes at once.
column28: True. One chromosome carries hundreds of genes, so losing, copying, flipping or moving a big piece can change many genes together. A point mutation affects only one base in one gene.
column29: How many genes sit on one chromosome?

column9: At the dentist, you wear a heavy lead apron while X-rays of your teeth are taken. Why?
column14: X-rays are a mutagen, and the apron keeps them from reaching the DNA in the rest of your body
column15: The apron keeps you warm in the cold office
column16: X-rays only work if the body is covered
column17: The apron keeps your clothes clean
column28: X-rays carry enough energy to damage DNA, so the apron shields your organs, including the sex cells. Thinking X-rays are harmless because doctors use them is the common mistake; small doses are low risk, but X-rays are still a mutagen.
column29: What can X-rays do to DNA?

column9: Which of these are gene mutations (changes to a few bases in one gene) rather than chromosomal mutations? Select all that apply.
column14: Substitution of one base
column28: Substitutions, insertions and deletions of single bases happen inside one gene. Inversions and translocations flip or move big chunks of a chromosome. The word deletion can name either kind, which is the common trap; a one-base deletion is a gene mutation.
column29: Look for changes measured in bases, not in big chromosome pieces.

column9: Why are mutations important for evolution?
column14: They create new variations in DNA that natural selection can act on
column15: They make every organism in a species identical
column16: They only happen to organisms that are already well adapted
column28: Mutations are the original source of new alleles, and natural selection then keeps the helpful ones. Saying mutations always make organisms better is the common mistake; selection, not the mutation itself, picks the winners.
column29: Evolution needs differences between individuals. Where do new differences come from?

column9: Doctors say smoking raises the risk of lung cancer. How are the two connected?
column14: Chemicals in smoke are mutagens that damage DNA in lung cells, which can make cells divide out of control
column15: Smoke makes the lungs too warm for normal cells
column16: Smoke adds extra chromosomes to every cell in the body
column17: Smoke stops lung cells from making any mRNA
column28: Tobacco smoke contains chemicals that change DNA. If the damaged genes control cell division, cells can grow out of control into a tumor. The mutations happen in the lung cells the smoke touches, not in every cell of the body.
column29: Which cells does the smoke touch, and what can it do to their DNA?

column9: Cells have enzymes that check newly copied DNA and fix most mistakes. What would most likely happen if a cell's repair enzymes stopped working?
column14: Mutations would build up faster in that cell
column15: The cell could no longer copy its DNA at all
column16: The cell's DNA would turn into RNA
column28: Copying mistakes still happen, but nothing fixes them, so mutations pile up. Saying mutations would stop is the common mistake; repair enzymes remove mutations, they don't cause them.
column29: Repair enzymes are like a spell-checker. What happens to typos without one?

column9: Original DNA: TAC GGA. Mutated DNA: TAC GGT. Counting from the left, which base position (1 to 6) changed? (Enter a number.)
column28: Positions 1–5 (T, A, C, G, G) match; position 6 changed from A to T. One base swapped for another makes this a substitution.
column29: Line the two sequences up and check each base in order.

column9: Match each type of mutation to what it does to the protein.
column14: Silent :: The protein is unchanged
column15: Missense :: One amino acid is replaced by a different one
column16: Nonsense :: The protein stops too early
column17: Frameshift :: Every codon after the change is regrouped
column28: Silent keeps the same amino acid, missense gives a different amino acid, nonsense creates an early stop, and a frameshift (from an insertion or deletion) regroups every codon after it. Mixing up missense and nonsense is the most common mistake.
column29: Nonsense ends the message; missense just misses on one word.

column9: A model gene is written as the sentence THE ANT ATE THE JAM. After a mutation it reads THE ANT TAT ETH EJA M. What happened?
column14: One letter was inserted, shifting every word after it
column15: One letter was swapped for another
column17: The whole sentence was flipped backward
column28: An extra T was added after ANT, so every group of three after it shifted: an insertion that causes a frameshift. A swap would change one word and leave the rest readable.
column29: Count the letters before and after. Did the sentence get longer?

column9: The most common cystic fibrosis mutation deletes three bases in a row from the CFTR gene. What happens to the CFTR protein?
column14: It is missing one amino acid, but the rest of the chain is normal
column15: Every amino acid after the deletion is different
column16: It is exactly the same as the normal protein
column17: It stops right after the start codon
column28: Three bases is one codon's worth, so the reading frame stays in step and the protein just loses one amino acid. That one missing amino acid is enough to make the protein fold wrong. Calling it a frameshift is the common mistake.
column29: Is 3 a multiple of the number of bases in a codon?

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG CCU GAA UAA. Mutated mRNA: AUG CCU GAU UAA. Codons: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, GAA = Glu, GAU = Asp, UAA = stop. Which type of mutation is this?
column14: Silent
column28: The protein goes from Met–Pro–Glu to Met–Pro–Asp: one amino acid changed and the length stayed the same, so it's missense. It isn't a frameshift because both mRNAs have the same number of bases.
column29: Translate both mRNAs, then compare the amino acid chains.

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG UCU AGA CCA UGA codes for Met–Ser–Arg–Pro. A substitution changes the mRNA to AUG UCU UGA CCA UGA. Codons: UCU = Ser, AGA = Arg, CCA = Pro, UGA = stop. What protein is made now?
column14: Met–Ser
column28: The third codon became UGA, a stop codon, so the ribosome stops after Met–Ser. Skipping the stop and continuing on to Pro (Met–Ser–Pro) is the common mistake: nothing after a stop codon is translated.
column29: Read codon by codon and stop the moment you reach a stop codon.

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC CGT ATT. A mutation changes it to TAC CGG ATT. Codons: GCA = Ala, GCC = Ala, UAA = stop. What is the effect on the protein?
column14: No change: a silent mutation
column15: One amino acid changes: a missense mutation
column16: The protein stops early: a nonsense mutation
column17: Every amino acid after it changes: a frameshift
column28: Transcribe first: CGT → GCA and CGG → GCC. Both code for Ala, so the protein doesn't change. Trying to read the DNA letters as codons without transcribing is the common mistake.
column29: Turn each DNA triplet into its mRNA codon first (A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C).

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG GGC AAA. A substitution changes the 5th base from G to A. Type the new second codon. ___
column28: Number the bases: A1 U2 G3 G4 G5 C6. Changing base 5 to A turns GGC into GAC. Changing the wrong base by miscounting is the common mistake.
column29: Number each base from the left, starting at 1.

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG UCA GGA CUU AAC UGA codes for Met–Ser–Gly–Leu–Asn. The first base of the second codon (the U in UCA) is deleted. Codons: CAG = Gln, GAC = Asp, UUA = Leu, ACU = Thr. What amino acid chain is made now (as far as the full codons go)?
column14: Met–Gln–Asp–Leu–Thr
column28: After the deletion the bases regroup as AUG CAG GAC UUA ACU GA, giving Met–Gln–Asp–Leu–Thr, so every amino acid after Met changed. Simply dropping Ser (Met–Gly–Leu–Asn) is the common mistake: a one-base deletion doesn't remove a whole codon.
column29: Write the mRNA without the deleted base, then split it into new groups of three starting at AUG.

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG CCA GUU CAU GGC UGA codes for Met–Pro–Val–His–Gly. An extra A is inserted right after the second codon. Codons: AGU = Ser, UCA = Ser, UGG = Trp, CUG = Leu. What chain is made now (as far as the full codons go)?
column14: Met–Pro–Ser–Ser–Trp–Leu
column28: The new mRNA regroups as AUG CCA AGU UCA UGG CUG A, so everything after Pro changes. Adding one new amino acid and keeping the rest (Met–Pro–Lys–Val–His–Gly) is the common mistake; that would take three inserted bases.
column29: Rewrite the mRNA with the extra A, then regroup in threes from AUG.

column9: A gene's mRNA codes for a protein 150 amino acids long. A substitution turns codon 40 into a stop codon. How many amino acids long is the shortened protein? (Enter a number.)
column28: Codons 1 through 39 are translated, and codon 40 is now a stop, so the chain has 39 amino acids. Answering 40 is the common mistake: a stop codon doesn't add an amino acid.
column29: The ribosome stops when it reaches codon 40. How many codons came before it?

column9: A deletion removes exactly 4 amino acids from a protein without causing a frameshift. How many bases were deleted from the gene? (Enter a number.)
column28: Each amino acid comes from one codon of 3 bases, so 4 × 3 = 12 bases. Answering 4 is the common mistake; deleting 4 bases would shift the frame.
column29: How many bases code for one amino acid?

column9: Put these mutations in order from the LEAST change to the protein to the MOST change.
column14: A one-base deletion right after the start codon
column28: Silent changes nothing, missense changes one amino acid, and a one-base deletion right after the start codon shifts the frame for almost the whole protein. Ranking a missense as worse than an early frameshift is the common mistake.
column29: Count how many amino acids each one changes.

column9: Why does a one-base deletion near the start of a gene usually do more damage than the same deletion near the end?
column14: More codons come after it, so more of the protein is read in the wrong frame
column15: Deletions near the start always remove more bases
column16: The start of a gene has no codons
column17: Ribosomes read genes from the end backward
column28: A frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Near the start, that's nearly the whole protein; near the end, it's just the last few amino acids. Ribosomes read from the start codon forward, not backward.
column29: A frameshift affects everything after it. How much comes after it in each case?

column9: Two non-matching chromosomes start as ABCDEFG and MNOPQRS (each letter is a gene). After a mutation they read ABCDRS and MNOPQEFG. Which mutation happened?
column14: Inversion
column28: Pieces traded places between two different chromosomes: EFG moved onto the second chromosome and RS moved onto the first. That's a translocation. Calling it a deletion because ABCDEFG got shorter is the common mistake; the genes weren't lost, they moved.
column29: Track where genes E, F and G ended up.

column9: A normal chromosome reads ABCDEFGH. Which of these mutated chromosomes shows an inversion?
column14: ABCFGH
column28: In ABEDCFGH the section CDE is still there but reads EDC, backward: an inversion. ABCFGH is a deletion, ABCDEFEFGH is a duplication, and ABCDXYZ has genes from another chromosome (a translocation).
column29: Look for the version that has all the same genes, with some of them in reverse order.

column9: A normal chromosome reads ABCDEF (each letter is a gene). Match each mutated chromosome to the mutation it shows.
column14: ABDEF :: Deletion
column17: ABCXY, where X and Y came from a different chromosome :: Translocation
column28: ABDEF lost C (deletion), ABCBCDEF has BC twice (duplication), ADCBEF has BCD reversed (inversion), and ABCXY picked up genes from a different chromosome (translocation). Confusing inversion with translocation is the most common mistake.
column29: For each one, ask: was something lost, copied, flipped or brought in from elsewhere?

column9: A substitution happens in a stretch of DNA between two genes, where the DNA is not used to make any protein. What is the most likely effect on the organism's proteins?
column14: No effect, because no protein is coded by that DNA
column15: Every protein in the cell changes
column16: The nearest gene gets a frameshift
column28: If the DNA isn't part of a gene, no codon changes, so no protein changes and the mutation is most likely neutral. Assuming every mutation changes a protein is the common mistake.
column29: A protein only changes if one of its codons changes.

column9: In Huntington's disease, a gene has many extra copies of the codon CAG (which codes for glutamine, Gln) repeated in a row. What does this do to the protein?
column14: Extra Gln amino acids are added, but the rest of the protein reads normally
column15: Every amino acid after the repeats changes
column16: The protein ends right at the first CAG
column17: Nothing changes, because CAG is a normal codon
column28: Each CAG is a full codon, so the extra bases come in groups of three and the reading frame stays the same. The protein just gets a long run of extra Gln, which makes it clump in brain cells. Calling it a frameshift is the common mistake.
column29: How many bases does each extra copy add?

column9: The codon UGG codes for tryptophan (Trp). Which single-base change to UGG would cause a nonsense mutation? (Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.)
column14: UGA
column28: Changing the last G to A gives UGA, a stop codon. UGU (Cys), CGG (Arg) and UUG (Leu) all code for amino acids, so those changes would be missense.
column29: Compare each choice to the list of stop codons.

column9: The codon GGA codes for glycine (Gly). Gly is also coded by GGU, GGC and GGG. Which of these changes to GGA would be silent? Select all that apply.
column14: GGU
column28: GGU, GGC and GGG all still code for Gly, so the protein doesn't change. GAA (Glu) and AGA (Arg) would be missense, and UGA is a stop codon (nonsense).
column29: Only codons that still code for Gly keep the protein the same.

column9: A missense mutation changes one amino acid in the active site of an enzyme that breaks down a sugar. What is the most likely result?
column14: The enzyme may fold differently and work poorly or not at all
column15: The enzyme becomes twice as long
column16: Nothing, because one amino acid can't affect an enzyme
column17: The sugar turns into a protein
column28: An enzyme's shape depends on its amino acids, and the active site has to fit the sugar. Changing one amino acid there can change the fit, so the enzyme may stop working. Thinking one amino acid can't matter is the common mistake.
column29: Enzymes work because of their shape. What sets the shape?

column9: Why might a missense mutation sometimes have little or no noticeable effect?
column14: The new amino acid may be similar enough that the protein still folds and works
column15: Missense mutations never change the amino acid sequence
column16: The ribosome skips the changed codon
column17: The mRNA fixes the mistake before translation
column28: A missense mutation does change one amino acid, but if the new one has a similar size and chemistry, or sits in a part of the protein that isn't critical, the protein can still work. Saying missense never changes the sequence is the common mix-up with silent mutations.
column29: Is every part of a protein equally important to its shape?

column9: Most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after they are weaned. Many people have a mutation that keeps lactase working into adulthood. In a culture that raises dairy cows, how is this mutation best described?
column14: Helpful: adults can get nutrition from milk
column15: Harmful: it breaks the lactase enzyme
column16: Neutral: it has no effect on any protein
column17: It can't be described, because all mutations are harmful
column28: The mutation lets adults digest milk, which is an advantage where milk is a common food. It doesn't break lactase; it keeps it working longer. Assuming all mutations are harmful is the common mistake.
column29: Does this mutation help or hurt an adult who drinks milk?

column9: A mutation gives a snowshoe hare white fur all year instead of turning brown in summer. Which statement best describes whether the mutation is helpful or harmful?
column14: It depends on the environment: helpful where snow covers the ground most of the year, harmful where the ground is brown for months
column15: It is always helpful, because white fur is warmer
column16: It is always harmful, because all mutations are harmful
column17: It has no effect, because fur color isn't controlled by genes
column28: Camouflage only helps if the fur matches the background, so the same mutation can help in one place and hurt in another. Treating helpful or harmful as fixed, no matter the environment, is the common mistake.
column29: Picture a white hare on snow, then on brown dirt. Which one does a fox spot?

column9: In one type of leukemia, a piece of chromosome 9 and a piece of chromosome 22 break off and trade places. Which type of mutation is this?
column14: Inversion
column28: Pieces moving between two different chromosomes is a translocation. An inversion would flip a piece on the same chromosome, which is the common mix-up.
column29: How many different chromosomes are involved?

column9: A duplication gives a chromosome an extra copy of a gene. What is the most likely effect on that gene's protein?
column14: The cell may make more of that protein than normal
column15: The cell can no longer make that protein
column16: Every amino acid in the protein changes
column17: The protein turns into a stop codon
column28: Both copies of the gene can be transcribed, so the cell may make extra protein. The gene itself isn't changed, so the amino acid sequence stays the same; thinking a duplication scrambles the protein is the common mistake.
column29: Is the gene damaged, or is there just more of it?

column9: A DNA template strand has the triplet GGA. A substitution changes it to GGT. Type the mRNA codon made from the mutated triplet. ___
column28: G→C, G→C, T→A gives CCA. Writing GGU (copying the DNA and only swapping T for U) is the common mistake; the mRNA is complementary to the template.
column29: Pair each template base: A→U, T→A, C→G, G→C.

column9: A normal protein is 120 amino acids long. A mutation inserts 9 bases into the middle of its gene, and none of the new codons is a stop codon. How many amino acids long is the new protein? (Enter a number.)
column28: 9 bases = 3 codons, so 3 amino acids are added and the frame isn't shifted: 120 + 3 = 123. Adding 9 (one per base) is the common mistake.
column29: Convert bases to codons first.

column9: Two fruit flies each have one mutation at codon 5 of the same 300-codon eye-color gene. Fly 1 has a substitution, and Fly 2 has a deletion of one base. Whose eye-color protein is most likely to be more different from normal, and why?
column14: Fly 2, because the deletion shifts the reading frame for every codon after codon 5
column15: Fly 1, because substitutions always make stop codons
column16: Fly 1, because substitutions change every codon after the mutation
column17: Neither; they are equally changed, because both mutations involve one base
column28: A substitution changes at most one codon, but deleting one base regroups all the codons after it. Thinking one base is one base, so the effects must be equal, is the common mistake.
column29: Which mutation changes only one codon, and which changes the grouping of all the codons after it?

column9: A scientist wants to test whether a chemical in a weed killer is a mutagen. She grows two groups of bacteria, one with the chemical and one without. Why does she need the group without the chemical?
column14: To compare against, so she can tell whether the chemical caused extra mutations
column15: To give the bacteria more food
column16: Because bacteria can't grow with the chemical
column17: To make sure every bacterium mutates
column28: The group without the chemical is the control. Mutations happen at a low rate even without mutagens, so she needs that normal rate before she can say the chemical raised it. Forgetting that mutations happen naturally is the common mistake.
column29: How would she know what the normal number of mutations is?

column9: You are given a normal and a mutated DNA template strand. Put the steps in order to predict how the mutation affects the protein.
column14: Translate each mRNA codon into an amino acid
column15: Classify the mutation as silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift
column16: Transcribe the mutated DNA into mRNA
column17: Compare the new amino acid chain with the normal chain
column28: DNA must be transcribed into mRNA before its codons can be translated; then you compare the chains and name the effect. Translating straight from the DNA is the common mistake.
column29: You need amino acids before you can compare them, and mRNA before you can get amino acids.

column9: Two different substitutions happen in the mRNA codon UAC (tyrosine, Tyr). Mutation 1 changes it to UAU, which also codes for Tyr. Mutation 2 changes it to UAA, a stop codon. Which statement is correct?
column14: Mutation 1 is silent and mutation 2 is nonsense
column15: Mutation 1 is missense and mutation 2 is silent
column28: UAC to UAU keeps Tyr (silent). UAC to UAA makes a stop codon (nonsense). Both are substitutions, so neither one shifts the reading frame.
column29: Handle each mutation separately: same amino acid, different amino acid, or stop?

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC GTT CCA ACT. A mutation changes it to TAC ATT CCA ACT. Codons: AUG = Met, CAA = Gln, GGU = Gly, and UAA, UAG and UGA = stop. What is the effect?
column14: Nonsense: the protein is just Met
column15: Missense: Gln is swapped for another amino acid
column16: Silent: the protein is still Met–Gln–Gly
column17: Frameshift: every amino acid after Met changes
column28: Transcribe: normal mRNA AUG CAA GGU UGA (Met–Gln–Gly); mutated mRNA AUG UAA GGU UGA. UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends after Met. It isn't a frameshift because the number of bases didn't change.
column29: Transcribe both strands before translating. Watch for a stop codon.

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC AAA CGG TCT ATT. The first A of the second triplet is deleted. Codons: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GCC = Ala, AGA = Arg, UUG = Leu, CCA = Pro, GAU = Asp, UAA = stop. What does the mutated gene code for (as far as the full codons go)?
column14: Met–Leu–Pro–Asp
column28: Mutated DNA: TAC AAC GGT CTA TT, so the mRNA is AUG UUG CCA GAU AA → Met–Leu–Pro–Asp. The normal chain is Met–Phe–Ala–Arg, so every amino acid after Met changed and the stop codon was lost. Dropping just Phe (Met–Ala–Arg) is the common mistake; a one-base deletion doesn't remove a whole codon.
column29: Delete the base in the DNA, regroup in threes, then transcribe and translate.

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG GAU ACU AGC UUC UAA. Mutated mRNA: AUG GAU CUA GCU UCU AA. Which statement correctly describes this mutation?
column14: A one-base deletion that shifts the reading frame, so the codons after GAU are all different
column15: A substitution that changes only the third codon
column16: A one-base insertion that adds one amino acid
column17: A three-base deletion that removes one codon
column28: The mutated mRNA has 17 bases instead of 18: the A at the start of the third codon was deleted. Every codon after GAU is regrouped (CUA GCU UCU), and the stop codon UAA is lost. Seeing CUA where ACU used to be and calling it a substitution is the common mistake; count the bases first.
column29: Count the bases in each mRNA before comparing codons.

column9: An mRNA has 300 codons, counting the stop codon at the end. A substitution turns codon 81 into a stop codon. How many fewer amino acids does the mutated protein have than the normal protein? (Enter a number.)
column28: The normal protein has 299 amino acids (the stop codon adds none). The mutated protein has 80 (codons 1–80). 299 − 80 = 219. Answering 220 is the common mistake that comes from counting the stop codon as an amino acid.
column29: Find the length of each protein first. Stop codons don't add an amino acid.

column9: Which of these changes to a gene would shift the reading frame, changing how every codon after it is read? Select all that apply.
column14: Inserting 1 base
column28: The frame shifts whenever the number of bases added or removed is not a multiple of 3: 1, 2 and 4 shift it, while 3 and 6 add or remove whole codons. A substitution doesn't change the count at all. Thinking every insertion or deletion is a frameshift is the common mistake.
column29: Ask whether each number divides evenly by 3.

column9: A student says, "A mutation that changes only one base can't really hurt an organism." Which evidence best shows the student is wrong?
column14: A single-base substitution can create a stop codon near the start of a gene, making a protein too short to work
column15: Silent mutations show that one base never matters
column16: Chromosomal mutations change much larger pieces of DNA
column17: UV light can cause mutations in skin cells
column28: One base can turn a codon into a stop codon, so the protein ends early and usually can't do its job. Choice c is true, but it doesn't address one-base changes, which is the common trap: a true statement that doesn't answer the claim.
column29: Pick the evidence that is about a one-base change and shows harm.

column9: A normal protein reads Met–Thr–Gly–Leu–Pro–Val–His. A mutant version of the protein reads Met–Thr–Asp–Phe–Gln–Tyr–Ile. Which mutation most likely caused this?
column14: A one-base insertion or deletion in codon 3, which shifted the reading frame
column28: Every amino acid from position 3 on is different, which is the signature of a frameshift. A missense mutation would change only Gly, a silent one would change nothing, and a nonsense one would cut the chain short instead of changing it. Choosing missense because the change starts at one codon is the common mistake.
column29: Count how many amino acids changed. One, or all of them after a certain point?

column9: A normal protein reads Met–Ser–Asp–Phe–Lys–Ala–Gly. A mutant reads Met–Ser–Asp–Phe–Ala–Gly. Everything else about the protein is the same. Which mutation best explains this?
column14: Three bases (one codon) were deleted
column15: One base was deleted, shifting the frame
column28: Only Lys is missing and every amino acid after it is unchanged, so the reading frame was not disturbed. That points to losing exactly one codon (three bases). A one-base deletion would scramble the amino acids after Phe, which is the common mistake.
column29: If the frame had shifted, would Ala and Gly still be there?

column9: Each mutation below happens in codon 2 (GAA) of a gene. Match each one to its effect. Codon key: GAA and GAG = Glu, GCA = Ala, UAA = stop.
column14: GAA changes to GAG :: Silent: the protein is unchanged
column15: GAA changes to GCA :: Missense: one amino acid is different
column16: GAA changes to UAA :: Nonsense: the protein ends early
column17: The first G of GAA is deleted :: Frameshift: the codons after it are regrouped
column28: GAG is still Glu (silent), GCA is Ala (missense), UAA is a stop codon (nonsense), and losing a base regroups everything after it (frameshift). Mixing up missense and nonsense is the most common mistake.
column29: For each change, ask: same amino acid, a new amino acid, a stop, or a change in the number of bases?

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC GGA CTT AAA ACT. An extra G is inserted right after the first triplet (after TAC). Codons: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, CCC = Pro, GAA = Glu, UUU = Phe, and UAA, UAG and UGA = stop. What does the mutated gene code for?
column14: Met–Pro, then stop
column28: The mutated DNA TAC GGG ACT TAA AAC T transcribes to AUG CCC UGA AUU UUG A. CCC is Pro and UGA is a stop, so the chain is just Met–Pro: the frameshift created an early stop. Adding one Pro and keeping the rest (Met–Pro–Pro–Glu–Phe) is the common mistake.
column29: Insert the G in the DNA, regroup in threes, transcribe, then translate until you reach a stop.

column9: Normal mRNA: AUG AAA CCC GGG UUU. The first A of the second codon is deleted. Type the new third codon. ___
column28: Without that A, the mRNA is AUGAACCCGGGUUU, which regroups as AUG AAC CCG GGU UU. The third codon is CCG. Answering CCC (the old third codon) is the common mistake: after a deletion, every codon downstream changes.
column29: Rewrite the whole mRNA without the deleted base, then split it into threes from the start.

column9: An mRNA reads AUG GCU AAC GAG CUU UGG UAA and codes for 6 amino acids. An extra A is inserted right after the start codon AUG. How many amino acids will the mutated protein have? (Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA.) (Enter a number.)
column28: The new mRNA reads AUG AGC UAA CGA GCU UUG GUA A. The third codon is now UAA, a stop codon, so only two amino acids (Met and Ser) are made. Answering 7 (one extra amino acid) is the common mistake; one extra base shifts the frame instead.
column29: Rewrite with the extra A, regroup in threes, and count codons until the first stop.

column9: During meiosis, two matching chromosomes (both ABCDEFGH) break and rejoin unevenly. Afterward, chromosome 1 reads ABCDEFEFGH and chromosome 2 reads ABCDGH. What happened to each chromosome?
column14: Chromosome 1 has a duplication; chromosome 2 has a deletion
column15: Chromosome 1 has a deletion; chromosome 2 has a duplication
column17: Chromosome 1 has a translocation; chromosome 2 has an inversion
column28: Chromosome 1 has EF twice (duplication) and chromosome 2 is missing EF (deletion): the genes one chromosome gained are the ones the other lost. Swapping the two labels is the common mistake, so check which one got longer.
column29: Which chromosome got longer, and which got shorter?

column9: Look at these codons: GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for Ala; CUU, CUC, CUA and CUG all code for Leu; GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for Gly. Based on this pattern, a substitution in which base of a codon is most likely to be silent?
column14: The third (last) base
column17: All three positions are equally likely to be silent
column28: In each set, the first two bases stay the same and only the third base varies, so changing the third base often keeps the same amino acid. Changing the first or second base usually changes the amino acid. Assuming every position is equal is the common mistake.
column29: In each group of four codons, which position is the one that changes?

column9: Three bases are inserted into the middle of codon 10 of a gene (between its first and second bases). What is the most likely effect on the protein?
column14: One or two amino acids near codon 10 change or are added, but the codons after that read normally
column15: Every amino acid after codon 10 changes
column16: The protein is always exactly the same
column17: The protein loses every amino acid after codon 10
column28: Three bases add one codon's worth, so the frame is back in step right after the insertion. Only the split codon and the new codon are affected (unless one of them happens to be a stop). Calling it a frameshift because it landed in the middle of a codon is the common mistake.
column29: Write codon 10 as three letters, slip three new letters between its first and second, and regroup.

column9: A gene already has a one-base insertion near its start. Which second mutation, close by, would most likely put the rest of the protein back in the correct reading frame?
column14: A one-base deletion
column28: +1 and −1 cancel, so after the second mutation the codons line up again and only the codons between the two mutations are changed. Another insertion makes the total +2, a substitution doesn't change the count, and a two-base deletion overshoots to −1.
column29: Add up the bases gained and lost. When is the total a multiple of 3?

column9: Which statement best explains why mutations that change a protein are more often harmful than helpful?
column14: Proteins already work well, so a random change is more likely to break one than improve it
column15: Mutations only happen in genes that are already broken
column16: Cells make harmful mutations on purpose
column28: A working protein is like a working machine: changing a random part usually makes it worse, though once in a while it helps. Helpful mutations aren't silent; silent ones don't change the protein at all, which is the common mix-up.
column29: Imagine changing a random part inside a phone that already works.

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC TTG CGA ATC. A mutation changes it to TAC TTC CGA ATC. Codons: AUG = Met, AAC = Asn, AAG = Lys, GCU = Ala, UAG = stop. What is the effect on the protein?
column14: Missense: Asn is replaced by Lys
column16: Nonsense: the protein stops after Met
column17: Frameshift: Ala and everything after it change
column28: Normal mRNA AUG AAC GCU UAG gives Met–Asn–Ala; mutated mRNA AUG AAG GCU UAG gives Met–Lys–Ala. One amino acid changed, so it's missense. Skipping transcription and trying to read TTC as a codon is the common mistake.
column29: Transcribe the changed triplet, then look it up in the codon key.

column9: A one-base deletion happens in codon 3 of a gene that is 100 codons long. Which outcomes are possible? Select all that apply.
column14: Most amino acids after codon 3 change
column17: Only amino acid 3 changes, and the rest stay normal
column18: The protein is guaranteed to be identical to normal
column28: A frameshift this early regroups almost every codon, often runs into a stop codon soon, and usually ruins the protein. It can't change only one amino acid or leave the protein identical; those describe substitutions, which is the common mix-up.
column29: A frameshift affects everything downstream. What could show up when codons are regrouped?

column9: A class tests whether UV light is a mutagen. They spread equal amounts of yeast on 10 plates, put 5 plates under a UV lamp for 30 seconds, and keep 5 in the dark. Which result would best support the claim that UV light causes mutations?
column14: The UV plates average many more mutant colonies than the dark plates
column15: Both groups have the same number of mutant colonies
column16: The dark plates have more mutant colonies
column17: The UV plates are warmer than the dark plates
column28: If UV is a mutagen, the UV plates should have clearly more mutants than the control plates. Equal numbers would mean UV made no difference, and temperature isn't a measure of mutations.
column29: What would you expect to see if UV adds mutations above the normal rate?

column9: A plate of E. coli bacteria exposed to X-rays grew 250 mutant colonies. A control plate with no X-rays grew 10 mutant colonies. How many times more mutant colonies grew on the X-ray plate? (Enter a number.)
column28: 250 ÷ 10 = 25, so the X-ray plate had 25 times as many mutants. Subtracting (240) is the common mistake; "how many times" asks you to divide. The control shows that a few mutations happen even with no mutagen.
column29: "How many times more" means divide.

column9: A translocation breaks a chromosome right in the middle of a gene, so the first half of that gene is joined to DNA from a different chromosome. What is the most likely result?
column14: The protein from that gene is changed or not made correctly, because the gene was split
column15: No genes are affected, because translocations only move whole chromosomes
column16: Only one base in the gene changes
column17: The organism gains a copy of every gene
column28: If the break lands inside a gene, half of the gene is now attached to unrelated DNA, so the protein made from it is different (this is what happens in the chromosome 9 and 22 leukemia). Thinking chromosomal mutations never change individual genes is the common mistake.
column29: What happens to a recipe if you cut it in half and tape the end of a different recipe onto it?

column9: Put these events in order to explain how one base change leads to sickle cell disease.
column14: Red blood cells bend into a stiff sickle shape
column15: One base in the hemoglobin gene is substituted
column16: Hemoglobin molecules clump together inside red blood cells
column17: The mRNA codon changes, so one amino acid in hemoglobin is replaced
column18: Sickled cells get stuck in small blood vessels and block blood flow
column28: Gene → mRNA → amino acid → protein → cell shape → health problem. Putting the cell shape before the hemoglobin change is the common mistake; the cells sickle because the hemoglobin inside them clumps.
column29: Start with the DNA and end with the symptom.

column9: A student claims, "A frameshift is always worse than a nonsense mutation." Gene X has a nonsense mutation at codon 5 of 400. Gene Y has a one-base deletion at codon 398 of 400. Which evaluation is best?
column14: The claim is wrong here: Gene X loses almost all of its protein, while Gene Y changes only the very end of its protein
column15: The claim is right: Gene Y is worse because every frameshift ruins the whole protein
column16: The claim is right: Gene X is unchanged because nonsense mutations are silent
column17: Both genes are equally affected because each has one mutation
column28: Position matters. A stop at codon 5 leaves a 4-amino-acid stub, so almost all of gene X's protein is gone. A frameshift at codon 398 can only change the very end of the protein, from codon 398 on. "Frameshifts are always worst" is a rule of thumb, not a law.
column29: For each gene, count how many codons the mutation affects.

column9: A gene's normal mRNA, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 600 bases long. A mutation deletes 3 bases that make up one whole codon in the middle. How many amino acids long is the mutated protein? (Enter a number.)
column28: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 codons, and one of them is the stop codon, so the normal protein has 199 amino acids. Losing one whole codon removes one amino acid: 198. Answering 199 (counting the stop codon as an amino acid) or 597 (counting bases instead of codons) are the common mistakes.
column29: Bases → codons → amino acids. Don't count the stop codon as an amino acid.
